A 33-year-old primigravida at 12 weeks gestation presents for her initial prenatal visit. Her medical
history includes a previous loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) for cervical dysplasia and
well-controlled mild intermittent asthma. She reports breast tenderness, decreased exercise tolerance,
and concerns about preterm birth due to her prior cervical procedure. Her vital signs are stable, and
physical examination reveals a palpable uterine fundus at the pelvic brim. Pelvic examination shows
normal external genitalia, a slightly soft and closed cervix, appropriately sized uterus for gestational
age, and no adnexal masses. What is the most appropriate method for assessing potential cervical
incompetence in this patient? Answer Choices: (A) Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pelvis (B)
Amniocentesis to assess fetal lung maturity (C) Transabdominal ultrasound at 12 weeks gestation (D)
Digital cervical examination at 24 weeks gestation (E) Physical exam with cervical length measurement
at 20 weeks gestation (F) Transvaginal ultrasound at 18 weeks gestation (G) Serial transvaginal
ultrasounds starting at 16 weeks gestation (H) Abdominal ultrasound at 18 weeks gestation (I)
Transvaginal ultrasound in the first trimester (J) Cervical biopsy and histologic evaluation
 A. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pelvis
B. Serial transvaginal ultrasounds starting at 16 weeks gestation
C. Amniocentesis to assess fetal lung maturity
D. Transvaginal ultrasound at 18 weeks gestation
E. Abdominal ultrasound at 18 weeks gestation
F. Physical exam with cervical length measurement at 20 weeks gestation
G. Digital cervical examination at 24 weeks gestation
H. Cervical biopsy and histologic evaluation
I. Transvaginal ultrasound in the first trimester
J. Transabdominal ultrasound at 12 weeks gestation
